questions.questionTextEn:
The following dipeptide derivative (aspartame) is used as an artificial sweetener:

$\mathrm{HO_2C-CH_2-CH(NH_2)-C(=O)-NH-CH(CH_2Ph)-C(=O)OCH_3}$ (the methyl ester of the dipeptide formed between an $N$-terminal amino acid having a $-\mathrm{CH_2CO_2H}$ side chain and a $C$-terminal amino acid having a $-\mathrm{CH_2Ph}$ benzyl side chain, both in the $S$/L-configuration).

The constituent $\alpha$-amino acids of this dipeptide are
questions.explanationEn:
The given artificial sweetener is **aspartame** ($N$-L-$\alpha$-aspartyl-L-phenylalanine 1-methyl ester). Hydrolyzing the central amide (peptide) bond and the methyl ester yields two $\alpha$-amino acids:
1. From the $N$-terminal residue: $\mathrm{HO_2C-CH_2-CH(NH_2)-CO_2H}$, which is **aspartic acid** (side chain $-\mathrm{CH_2CO_2H}$; glutamic acid would have $-\mathrm{CH_2CH_2CO_2H}$).
2. From the $C$-terminal residue: $\mathrm{Ph-CH_2-CH(NH_2)-CO_2H}$, which is **phenylalanine** (side chain $-\mathrm{CH_2Ph}$; tyrosine would have a *para*-hydroxy group on the phenyl ring).

Hence, the constituent $\alpha$-amino acids are **phenylalanine and aspartic acid** — Option **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The suitable reagent combination for the following transformation:

1-(1-methylcyclohexyl)ethan-1-one $\longrightarrow$ 1-methylcyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid

is
questions.explanationEn:
The starting material is a **methyl ketone**, 1-(1-methylcyclohexyl)ethan-1-one ($\mathrm{R-COCH_3}$, where $\mathrm{R} =$ 1-methylcyclohexyl), and the product is the corresponding carboxylic acid with one fewer carbon atom ($\mathrm{R-CO_2H}$).
- **Option (C):** Treatment with $\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}$ performs the **iodoform (haloform) reaction**: exhaustive $\alpha$-iodination of the $-\mathrm{COCH_3}$ group gives $\mathrm{R-C(=O)CI_3}$, followed by nucleophilic acyl substitution by $\mathrm{OH^-}$ to expel $\mathrm{CHI_3}$ and yield $\mathrm{R-CO_2^-Na^+}$. Acidic work-up with aq. $\mathrm{HCl}$ furnishes 1-methylcyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid.
- **Option (A):** Baeyer–Villiger oxidation with $m$-CPBA migrates the more substituted tertiary 1-methylcyclohexyl group preferentially over methyl, yielding 1-methylcyclohexyl acetate; subsequent hydrolysis gives 1-methylcyclohexanol and acetic acid instead.
- **Options (B) and (D):** $\mathrm{OsO_4}$ (dihydroxylation) and DMDO (epoxidation) are alkene oxidants and do not cleave a methyl ketone to a carboxylic acid.

Therefore, the correct option is **(C)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
For the reaction

$\mathrm{Ph-C(Me)_2-Br + KCN \xrightarrow{MeOH/H_2O} Ph-C(Me)_2-CN}$

if the concentration of $\mathrm{KCN}$ is increased four times, then the rate of the reaction would be
questions.explanationEn:
The substrate 2-bromo-2-phenylpropane ($\mathrm{Ph-C(Me)_2-Br}$) is a **tertiary benzylic bromide**. In a polar protic solvent mixture ($\mathrm{MeOH/H_2O}$), it undergoes nucleophilic substitution exclusively via the **unimolecular $\mathrm{S_N1}$ mechanism** because the tertiary benzylic carbocation $\mathrm{Ph-C^+(Me)_2}$ is strongly stabilized by both resonance and hyperconjugation, while steric hindrance prevents backside $\mathrm{S_N2}$ attack.

In an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ reaction, the rate-determining step is ionization of the substrate, so the rate law is first-order in substrate and zero-order in nucleophile:
$$\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{Ph-C(Me)_2-Br}]$$
Since $[\mathrm{KCN}]$ does not appear in the rate law, quadrupling $[\mathrm{KCN}]$ leaves the reaction rate **unaffected** — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the wavefunction $\psi(x) = N[\exp(ikx) + \exp(-ikx)]$. The complex conjugate $\psi^*(x)$ is

[Given: $N$ is the normalization constant; $i = \sqrt{-1}$]
questions.explanationEn:
To obtain the complex conjugate $\psi^*(x)$ of a wavefunction, replace every imaginary unit $i$ with $-i$ and replace any potentially complex constant $N$ with its complex conjugate $N^*$ (assuming $k$ and $x$ are real):
$$\psi^*(x) = N^*[\exp(-ikx) + \exp(+ikx)] = N^*[\exp(ikx) + \exp(-ikx)]$$
Note that $\exp(ikx) + \exp(-ikx) = 2\cos(kx)$ is purely real, so its complex conjugate is identical to itself, while $N$ becomes $N^*$.

Hence, the correct option is **(C)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Wavelength of X-rays used in a diffraction experiment is $1.54\ \text{\AA}$. X-rays are diffracted from a set of planes with an interplanar spacing of $1.54\ \text{\AA}$. Then the angle $\theta$ (in degrees) corresponding to the first-order Bragg diffraction is
questions.explanationEn:
By **Bragg's law** for X-ray diffraction:
$$n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$$
Given $n = 1$ (first-order diffraction), $\lambda = 1.54\ \text{\AA}$, and $d = 1.54\ \text{\AA}$:
$$\sin\theta = \frac{n\lambda}{2d} = \frac{1 \times 1.54\ \text{\AA}}{2 \times 1.54\ \text{\AA}} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5$$
$$\theta = \arcsin(0.5) = 30^\circ$$
Hence, the correct option is **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Identify the reaction for which, at equilibrium, a change in the volume of the closed reaction vessel at a constant temperature will not affect the extent of the reaction.
questions.explanationEn:
By **Le Chatelier's principle**, changing the volume (and hence total pressure) of a closed vessel at constant temperature has no effect on the equilibrium position only when the change in the number of moles of gaseous species is zero ($\Delta n_g = 0$):
- **(A)** $\Delta n_g = 1 - 0 = +1 \neq 0$
- **(B)** $\Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 1) = 0$ (volume change has no effect)
- **(C)** $\Delta n_g = 1 - 2 = -1 \neq 0$
- **(D)** $\Delta n_g = 1 - 0 = +1 \neq 0$

Therefore, the correct option is **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Among $[\mathrm{Ti(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}$, $[\mathrm{NiCl_4}]^{2-}$, $[\mathrm{CrO_4}]^{2-}$, and $[\mathrm{Mn(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$, the complex that exhibits the largest molar absorptivity in the visible region of the electronic absorption spectrum is
questions.explanationEn:
Molar absorptivity ($\varepsilon$) depends on the spin and Laporte selection rules:
- **$[\mathrm{CrO_4}]^{2-}$ ($\text{Cr}^{6+}$, $d^0$, tetrahedral):** Has no $d$-electrons; its intense yellow color arises from a **ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT)** transition ($\mathrm{O}(2p) \to \mathrm{Cr}(3d)$), which is both **spin-allowed and Laporte-allowed** ($\varepsilon \approx 10^3\text{--}10^4\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ cm^{-1}}$).
- **$[\mathrm{NiCl_4}]^{2-}$ ($d^8$, tetrahedral):** Lacks a center of inversion, so $d\text{--}p$ mixing relaxes the Laporte rule for spin-allowed $d\text{--}d$ transitions ($\varepsilon \approx 10^2\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ cm^{-1}}$).
- **$[\mathrm{Ti(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}$ ($d^1$, octahedral):** Spin-allowed but **Laporte-forbidden** $d\text{--}d$ transition ($\varepsilon \approx 5\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ cm^{-1}}$).
- **$[\mathrm{Mn(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ (high-spin $d^5$, octahedral):** Both **spin-forbidden and Laporte-forbidden** ($\varepsilon \approx 0.01\text{--}0.1\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ cm^{-1}}$).

Thus, $[\mathrm{CrO_4}]^{2-}$ has the largest molar absorptivity — Option **(C)**.

questions.questionTextEn: $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Br}$ and $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}$ are examples of
questions.explanationEn:
The two coordination compounds have the same molecular formula but differ in which anion is coordinated inside the inner sphere versus present as a free counter-ion outside:
- $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Br}$ ionizes in water to yield $\mathrm{Br^-}$ (gives a pale-yellow precipitate with $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$).
- $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}$ ionizes in water to yield $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ (gives a white precipitate with $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$).

Isomers that produce different ions in solution are called **ionization isomers** — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The pair of proteins having heme core is
questions.explanationEn:
Among oxygen-transport/storage metalloproteins:
- **Hemoglobin** and **myoglobin** both contain an iron(II)-protoporphyrin IX (**heme**) prosthetic group.
- **Hemerythrin** is a **non-heme** di-iron oxygen-binding protein.
- **Hemocyanin** is a **non-heme** di-copper oxygen-transport protein.

Hence, the pair having a heme core is **hemoglobin and myoglobin** — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The shape of $\mathrm{SCN^-}$ is
questions.explanationEn: The thiocyanate ion ($\mathrm{SCN^-}$) has $6 + 4 + 5 + 1 = 16$ valence electrons, making it isoelectronic with $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Its major resonance contributors are $[\mathrm{S=C=N}]^- \leftrightarrow [\mathrm{S-C\equiv N}]^-$. The central carbon atom forms two $\sigma$-bonds and has zero lone pairs ($sp$-hybridized, steric number 2), giving an $\mathrm{S-C-N}$ bond angle of $180^\circ$, i.e., a **linear** shape — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product formed in the following thermal reaction:

*cis*-1,2-bis($(E)$-prop-1-en-1-yl)cyclopropane (with both ring-junction $\mathrm{H}$ atoms *cis*/dashed and both $(E)$-propenyl groups *cis*) $\xrightarrow{\Delta}$

is
optionsEn: *trans*-3,4-dimethyltricyclo[4.1.0.0$^{2,5}$]heptane (intramolecular $[2+2]$ adduct with one $\mathrm{Me}$ group dashed and one wedged, *trans*)
questions.explanationEn:
*cis*-1,2-Divinylcyclopropanes undergo a facile, concerted thermal **$[3,3]$-sigmatropic Cope rearrangement** driven by relief of cyclopropane ring strain to form cyclohepta-1,4-dienes.
1. Because the two $(E)$-prop-1-en-1-yl groups are *cis* on the cyclopropane ring, the molecule adopts a **boat-like transition state** where both $(E)$-methyl groups project outward (*exo*) on the same face.
2. Breaking the C1–C2 cyclopropane bond and forming the new $\sigma$-bond between the terminal alkene carbons places both methyl groups on the **same face** (*cis*) of the resulting 7-membered ring.
3. Thermal $[2+2]$ cycloadditions (Options C and D) are symmetry-forbidden.

Thus, the major product is ***cis*-6,7-dimethylcyclohepta-1,4-diene** — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product formed in the following reaction:

2-methylpyridine $N$-oxide (2-picoline $N$-oxide) $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Ac_2O},\ \Delta}$

is
questions.explanationEn:
Heating 2-methylpyridine $N$-oxide with acetic anhydride ($\mathrm{Ac_2O}$) is the classic **Boekelheide rearrangement**:
1. Nucleophilic attack of the $N$-oxide oxygen on $\mathrm{Ac_2O}$ generates the $N$-acetoxy-2-methylpyridinium ion and acetate ($\mathrm{AcO^-}$).
2. Deprotonation of the acidic C2-methyl group by $\mathrm{AcO^-}$ forms an exocyclic 2-methylene-1-acetoxy-1,2-dihydropyridine intermediate.
3. Thermal rearrangement (via either a concerted $[3,3]$-sigmatropic shift or a tight ion/radical pair) cleaves the weak $\mathrm{N-O}$ bond and installs the acetoxy group onto the benzylic/picolylic carbon, rearomatizing the pyridine ring.

The major product is **(pyridin-2-yl)methyl acetate** — Option **(D)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product formed in the following reaction:

*cis*-1,2,3,4,4a,5,8,8a-octahydronaphthalene (*cis*-$\Delta^6$-octalin, fused cyclohexane–cyclohexene with *cis* ring-junction wedges) $\xrightarrow{\text{1. } \mathrm{O_3,\ Me_2S} \\ \text{2. aq. NaOH}}$

is
optionsEn: *cis*-3a,4,5,6,7,7a-hexahydro-1$H$-indene-2-carbaldehyde (fused cyclohexane and cyclopentene bearing a $-\mathrm{CHO}$ group at C2)
questions.explanationEn:
**Official IIT JAM 2024 CY Final Answer Key (IIT Madras): Marks to All (MTA).**

**Intended reaction pathway:**
1. **Step 1 ($\mathrm{O_3, Me_2S}$):** Reductive ozonolysis cleaves the cyclohexene $\mathrm{C=C}$ double bond of *cis*-1,2,3,4,4a,5,8,8a-octahydronaphthalene to yield the 1,6-dialdehyde, *cis*-2,2'-(cyclohexane-1,2-diyl)diacetaldehyde.
2. **Step 2 (aq. $\mathrm{NaOH}$):** Base-catalyzed intramolecular aldol addition of this 1,6-dialdehyde forms a 5-membered $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde, which upon dehydration gives the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated aldehyde in **Option (B)** (*cis*-3a,4,5,6,7,7a-hexahydro-1$H$-indene-2-carbaldehyde).

**Why IIT Madras awarded MTA:** Heating ($\Delta$) was omitted from Step 2 (`2. aq. NaOH`), making complete dehydration of the $\beta$-hydroxy aldol adduct to the enal in Option (B) ambiguous (and permitting competing aldol addition/Cannizzaro pathways under aqueous $\mathrm{NaOH}$ alone); additionally, the stereochemical wedges at the ring junction were drawn on the cyclohexane $\mathrm{C-C}$ bonds rather than the bridgehead $\mathrm{C-H}$ bonds. Consequently, the organizing institute declared this question **MTA (Marks to All)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
In the following reaction:

Optically pure *trans*-2-acetoxycyclohexyl *para*-toluenesulfonate (**X**, cyclohexane ring with dashed $-\mathrm{OTs}$ at C1 and wedged $-\mathrm{OAc}$ at C2) $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{AcOH/H_2O},\ \Delta}$

optically pure ester **X** formed product that did not exhibit optical rotation ($[\alpha]_D = 0$) due to the formation of

(Note: $\mathrm{Ts} =$ *para*-toluenesulfonyl; $\mathrm{Ac} =$ acetyl)
questions.explanationEn:
In optically pure *trans*-2-acetoxycyclohexyl tosylate (**X**), the $-\mathrm{OAc}$ and $-\mathrm{OTs}$ groups can adopt a *trans*-diaxial conformation.
1. **Neighboring group participation (anchimeric assistance):** The carbonyl oxygen of the $-\mathrm{OAc}$ group attacks C1 intramolecularly from the backside to displace $-\mathrm{OTs}$ with inversion, forming a **symmetrical (achiral, *meso*) cyclic acetoxonium ion** intermediate.
2. **Ring opening:** Subsequent nucleophilic attack by $\mathrm{AcOH}$ occurs with **equal probability** at C1 or C2 (both via backside $\mathrm{S_N2}$ attack, giving a second inversion = net retention of *trans* stereochemistry).
3. Attack at C1 yields one enantiomer of *trans*-1,2-diacetoxycyclohexane while attack at C2 yields its exact mirror image, producing a 50:50 **racemic mixture of *trans*-1,2-diacetoxycyclohexane** with $[\alpha]_D = 0$.

Hence, the correct option is **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major products **X** and **Y** in the following reactions:

- Reaction 1: A *trans*-decalin derivative bearing an angular axial-up $\mathrm{Me}$ at C10, an **equatorial $-\mathrm{OH}$** and **axial-down $-\mathrm{Me}$** at C2, and an **axial-up $-\mathrm{NH_2}$** and equatorial $-\mathrm{H}$ at C3 $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{HNO_2},\ 0\text{--}5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}}$ **X**
- Reaction 2: The C2 epimer (angular axial-up $\mathrm{Me}$ at C10, **equatorial $-\mathrm{Me}$** and **axial-down $-\mathrm{OH}$** at C2, and **axial-up $-\mathrm{NH_2}$** and equatorial $-\mathrm{H}$ at C3) $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{HNO_2},\ 0\text{--}5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}}$ **Y**

respectively, are
optionsEn: **X** = *trans*-decalin-2-one derivative (ketone at C2 with migrated equatorial $-\mathrm{Me}$ and axial-up $-\mathrm{H}$ at C3) and **Y** = *trans*-decalin $2\alpha,3\alpha$-epoxide (oxirane on the bottom face with equatorial $-\mathrm{Me}$ at C2)
**X** = *trans*-decalin-2-one derivative with axial-up $-\mathrm{Me}$ and equatorial $-\mathrm{H}$ at C3 and **Y** = *trans*-decalin aziridine
questions.explanationEn:
Diazotization of the axial-up $-\mathrm{NH_2}$ group with $\mathrm{HNO_2}$ at $0\text{--}5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ generates an axial-up diazonium ion ($-\mathrm{N_2^+}$). In a conformationally locked *trans*-decalin ring, the outcome is governed strictly by **stereoelectronic antiperiplanar (*trans*-diaxial) alignment** with the leaving $-\mathrm{N_2^+}$ group:
1. **Formation of X:** At C2, the **axial-down $-\mathrm{Me}$** group is antiperiplanar to the axial-up $-\mathrm{N_2^+}$ at C3. Therefore, a **semipinacol (1,2-methyl) shift** occurs with backside displacement of $\mathrm{N_2}$ (inversion at C3, placing the migrated $\mathrm{Me}$ equatorial and $\mathrm{H}$ axial-up), while the equatorial $-\mathrm{OH}$ at C2 forms a $\mathrm{C=O}$ ketone.
2. **Formation of Y:** In the C2 epimer, the **axial-down $-\mathrm{OH}$** group is antiperiplanar to the axial-up $-\mathrm{N_2^+}$ at C3. Intramolecular $\mathrm{S_N2}$ attack by the hydroxyl oxygen directly expels $\mathrm{N_2}$, forming the **$\alpha$-epoxide** on the bottom face while $-\mathrm{Me}$ remains equatorial.

Hence, the correct pair of major products is **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product formed in the following reaction sequence:

1,3-dithiane $\xrightarrow{\text{1. } \textit{sec}\text{-BuLi} \\ \text{2. } \mathrm{PhCH_2CH_2CH_2Br} \\ \text{3. } \mathrm{HgSO_4,\ aq.\ H_2SO_4} \\ \text{4. } \mathrm{MeOH,\ BF_3\cdot OEt_2}}$

is
questions.explanationEn:
This sequence illustrates the **Corey–Seebach umpolung** synthesis of an aldehyde followed by acetalization:
1. **Step 1 (*sec*-BuLi):** Deprotonates the acidic C2 position of 1,3-dithiane to form the 2-lithio-1,3-dithiane acyl anion equivalent.
2. **Step 2 ($\mathrm{PhCH_2CH_2CH_2Br}$):** $\mathrm{S_N2}$ alkylation with 1-bromo-3-phenylpropane gives 2-(3-phenylpropyl)-1,3-dithiane.
3. **Step 3 ($\mathrm{HgSO_4}$, aq. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$):** Thiophilic $\mathrm{Hg^{2+}}$-promoted hydrolysis unmasks the dithiane to the aldehyde, **4-phenylbutanal** ($\mathrm{PhCH_2CH_2CH_2CHO}$).
4. **Step 4 ($\mathrm{MeOH, BF_3\cdot OEt_2}$):** Lewis-acid-catalyzed acetalization converts 4-phenylbutanal into its dimethyl acetal, **1,1-dimethoxy-4-phenylbutane** ($\mathrm{PhCH_2CH_2CH_2CH(OMe)_2}$).

Hence, the correct option is **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The acidity of the compounds shown below:

- **I**: 1,2,3-trimethylcycloprop-1-ene (deprotonation of the C3 $\mathrm{C-H}$)
- **II**: cyclopenta-1,3-diene (deprotonation of the C5 $\mathrm{CH_2}$)
- **III**: benzene (deprotonation of an aromatic $\mathrm{C-H}$)
- **IV**: cyclohepta-1,3,5-triene (deprotonation of the C7 $\mathrm{CH_2}$)

follows the order
questions.explanationEn:
Acidity of each hydrocarbon is determined by the stability of its conjugate base (carbanion):
- **II (cyclopenta-1,3-diene, $\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 16$):** Deprotonation produces the planar, cyclic, conjugated $6\pi$-electron **aromatic** cyclopentadienyl anion $\implies$ **most acidic**.
- **IV (cyclohepta-1,3,5-triene, $\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 36\text{--}39$):** Deprotonation gives the $8\pi$-electron cycloheptatrienyl anion, which puckers out of planarity to avoid antiaromaticity and benefits from extended allylic/polyenyl delocalization $\implies$ second most acidic.
- **III (benzene, $\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 43$):** Deprotonation yields the localized $sp^2$-hybridized phenyl anion without additional resonance stabilization.
- **I (1,2,3-trimethylcycloprop-1-ene, $\mathrm{p}K_a > 60$):** Deprotonation generates a $4\pi$-electron **antiaromatic** cyclopropenyl anion, further destabilized by three electron-donating methyl groups $\implies$ **least acidic**.

Therefore, the acidity order is $\mathbf{II > IV > III > I}$ — Option **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product formed in the following reaction:

$(E)$-cinnamamide ($\mathrm{Ph-CH=CH-C(=O)NH_2}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{1. } \mathrm{Br_2,\ aq.\ KOH} \\ \text{2. aq. HCl}}$

is
questions.explanationEn:
1. **Step 1 ($\mathrm{Br_2}$, aq. $\mathrm{KOH}$):** The primary amide $(E)$-cinnamamide undergoes **Hofmann rearrangement** (loss of the carbonyl carbon as $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ via an isocyanate intermediate, $\mathrm{Ph-CH=CH-N=C=O}$) to form the vinylamine (enamine) $\mathrm{Ph-CH=CH-NH_2}$.
2. **Step 2 (aq. $\mathrm{HCl}$):** The enamine tautomerizes to the imine $\mathrm{Ph-CH_2-CH=NH}$, which rapidly hydrolyzes in aqueous acid to give **2-phenylacetaldehyde** ($\mathrm{PhCH_2CHO}$) and $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$.

Notice that one carbon atom is lost during the Hofmann degradation, ruling out the 3-carbon aldehyde in Option (A). Hence, the correct option is **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The ratio of osmotic pressures of aqueous solutions of $0.01\ \mathrm{M\ BaCl_2}$ to $0.005\ \mathrm{M\ NaCl}$ is

[Given: Both compounds dissociate completely in water]
questions.explanationEn:
Osmotic pressure is given by $\Pi = iCRT$. At the same temperature $T$, the ratio of osmotic pressures equals the ratio of effective molarities ($iC$):
- For $\mathrm{BaCl_2} \to \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-}$: complete dissociation gives van 't Hoff factor $i_1 = 3$, so $i_1 C_1 = 3 \times 0.01\ \mathrm{M} = 0.03\ \mathrm{M}$.
- For $\mathrm{NaCl} \to \mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}$: complete dissociation gives $i_2 = 2$, so $i_2 C_2 = 2 \times 0.005\ \mathrm{M} = 0.01\ \mathrm{M}$.

$$\frac{\Pi_{\mathrm{BaCl_2}}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{NaCl}}} = \frac{0.03}{0.01} = 3:1$$
Hence, the correct option is **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
In the cell reaction

$\mathrm{P^+(aq) + Q(s) \to P(s) + Q^+(aq)}$

the EMF of the cell, $E_{\text{cell}}$ is zero. The standard EMF of the cell, $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ is

[Given:
Activities of all solids are unity.
Activity of $\mathrm{P^+(aq)}$ is $2\ \mathrm{M}$. Activity of $\mathrm{Q^+(aq)}$ is $1\ \mathrm{M}$.
$R =$ universal gas constant; $T =$ temperature; $F =$ Faraday constant]
questions.explanationEn:
For the one-electron cell reaction $\mathrm{P^+(aq) + Q(s) \to P(s) + Q^+(aq)}$, $n = 1$, and the reaction quotient is:
$$Q_r = \frac{a_{\mathrm{P(s)}} \cdot a_{\mathrm{Q^+(aq)}}}{a_{\mathrm{P^+(aq)}} \cdot a_{\mathrm{Q(s)}}} = \frac{1 \times 1}{2 \times 1} = \frac{1}{2}$$
Applying the **Nernst equation** with $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$:
$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q_r \implies 0 = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$$
$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = -\frac{RT}{F}\ln(2)$$
Hence, the correct option is **(C)**.

questions.questionTextEn: If nitrogen and oxygen gases are at the same temperature, the correct statement according to the kinetic theory of gases is
optionsEn: Average kinetic energy of nitrogen and oxygen molecules is inversely proportional to temperature.
For nitrogen and oxygen molecules, the root mean square speed is equal to the most probable speed.
Average speed of nitrogen molecules is less than the average speed of oxygen molecules.
Average kinetic energies of nitrogen and oxygen molecules are equal.
questions.explanationEn:
According to the **kinetic theory of gases**:
- The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\langle E_k \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_B T$, which depends **only on absolute temperature $T$** and is independent of molar mass. Hence, at the same temperature, $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ have **equal average kinetic energies** — **(D) is correct**.
- **(A) is false:** $\langle E_k \rangle$ is *directly* proportional to $T$.
- **(B) is false:** $v_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M} > v_{\mathrm{mp}} = \sqrt{2RT/M}$.
- **(C) is false:** $v_{\mathrm{avg}} = \sqrt{8RT/(\pi M)}$; since $M(\mathrm{N_2}) = 28 < M(\mathrm{O_2}) = 32$, $\mathrm{N_2}$ has a *greater* average speed than $\mathrm{O_2}$.

Thus, the correct option is **(D)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
A system undergoes one clockwise cycle from point X back to point X on a Pressure ($y$-axis) versus Volume ($x$-axis) diagram (a closed loop traversed clockwise: expanding at higher pressure along the upper path and compressing at lower pressure along the lower path).

The correct statement about this process is
optionsEn: Internal energy of the system decreases at the end of the cycle.
Entropy of the system increases at the end of the cycle.
System performs work on the surroundings during the cycle.
Heat exchanged between system and surroundings is zero during the cycle.
questions.explanationEn:
For any complete **cyclic process** returning to the initial state X:
- Both internal energy ($U$) and entropy ($S$) are **state functions**, so $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0$ and $\Delta S_{\text{cycle}} = 0$. This rules out **(A)** and **(B)**.
- In a **clockwise** cycle on a $P\text{--}V$ diagram, expansion occurs at a higher pressure than compression. Thus, the net work performed **by** the system on the surroundings is positive:
$$W_{\text{by}} = \oint P\,dV = +\text{(enclosed area)} > 0$$
Hence, the system performs net work on the surroundings — **(C) is correct**.
- By the First Law ($\Delta U = Q - W_{\text{by}} = 0$), the net heat absorbed is $Q = W_{\text{by}} > 0 \neq 0$, ruling out **(D)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
For the reaction shown below:

$\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Mn_2(CO)_{10}} + \mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na[Mn(CO)_5]}$ (**P**) $\xrightarrow[\mathrm{-NaCl}]{\mathrm{CH_3Cl}}$ $[\mathrm{CH_3Mn(CO)_5}]$ (**Q**)

the oxidation states of $\mathrm{Mn}$ in **P** and **Q**, respectively, are
questions.explanationEn:
In both carbonyl complexes, $\mathrm{CO}$ is a neutral ligand (charge $= 0$):
1. **In P ($\mathrm{Na[Mn(CO)_5]}$):** The complex anion is $[\mathrm{Mn(CO)_5}]^-$. Let the oxidation state of $\mathrm{Mn}$ be $x$:
$$x + 5(0) = -1 \implies x = -1$$
2. **In Q ($[\mathrm{CH_3Mn(CO)_5}]$):** The methyl ligand ($\mathrm{CH_3^-}$) is treated as a $-1$ anionic X-type ligand in formal oxidation-state counting. Let the oxidation state of $\mathrm{Mn}$ be $y$:
$$y + (-1) + 5(0) = 0 \implies y = +1$$

Therefore, the oxidation states of $\mathrm{Mn}$ in **P** and **Q** are **$-1$ and $+1$**, respectively — Option **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The number and nature of $d\text{--}d$ transition(s) in the case of $\mathrm{Sc^{2+}}$ in an octahedral crystal field, respectively, are

[Ignore spin-orbit coupling and Jahn-Teller distortion.]
questions.explanationEn:
Scandium has atomic number $Z = 21$ ($[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^14s^2$), so $\mathrm{Sc^{2+}}$ has a **$3d^1$** electronic configuration.
1. **Number of transitions:** In an octahedral ($O_h$) crystal field, the $d$-orbitals split into $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$. The single electron occupies $t_{2g}$ ($^2T_{2g}$ ground term) and has only **1** possible $d\text{--}d$ transition: $^2T_{2g} \to {^2E_g}$.
2. **Nature of transition:** Both ground and excited states have $S = 1/2$ ($\Delta S = 0$), so the transition is **spin-allowed**. Because an octahedral complex has a center of inversion ($i$), a $g \to g$ ($d \to d$) transition is **Laporte-forbidden**.

Hence, the correct option is **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The $d\text{--}d$ transitions in $[\mathrm{Mn(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ and $[\mathrm{Ti(H_2O)_4}]^{3+}$, respectively, are

[Ignore spin-orbit coupling and Jahn-Teller distortion.]
questions.explanationEn:
The Laporte (symmetry) selection rule forbids $g \to g$ transitions in **centrosymmetric** complexes (those possessing an inversion center $i$):
1. **$[\mathrm{Mn(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ (octahedral, $O_h$):** Possesses a center of inversion ($i$), so all $d\text{--}d$ transitions are **symmetry (Laporte) forbidden** (as well as spin-forbidden for high-spin $d^5$).
2. **$[\mathrm{Ti(H_2O)_4}]^{3+}$ (tetrahedral, $T_d$):** Lacks a center of inversion; its $t_2$ ($d$-orbitals) mix with $t_2$ ($p$-orbitals), making the $e \to t_2$ ($^2E \to {^2T_2}$) transition **symmetry allowed** (since the direct product $E \otimes T_2 \otimes T_2$ contains the totally symmetric representation $A_1$ in $T_d$).

Thus, the transitions are **symmetry forbidden and symmetry allowed**, respectively — Option **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn: A pair of isosteric compounds is
questions.explanationEn:
**Isosteric compounds** (isosteres) have the same number of atoms, the same number of valence (and total) electrons, and analogous molecular structures:
- **$\mathrm{H_3N\cdot BH_3}$ (ammonia borane):** $8$ atoms; valence electrons $= 5 + 3 + 6(1) = 14$; total electrons $= 7 + 5 + 6 = 18$; staggered tetrahedral ethane-like geometry.
- **$\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ (ethane):** $8$ atoms; valence electrons $= 2(4) + 6(1) = 14$; total electrons $= 2(6) + 6 = 18$; staggered tetrahedral geometry.
- By contrast, $\mathrm{H_2NBH_2}$ has 6 atoms (isoelectronic with $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$), and $\mathrm{B_2H_6}$ has only 12 valence electrons (electron-deficient, bridged structure).

Hence, $\mathrm{H_3N\cdot BH_3}$ and $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ form an isosteric pair — Option **(B)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
$\mathrm{Zn-C}$ bond polarity in the compounds below:

- **I**: $\mathrm{HC\equiv C-Zn-C\equiv CH}$ (diethynylzinc, $sp$-hybridized $\mathrm{C}$)
- **II**: $\mathrm{H_2C=CH-Zn-CH=CH_2}$ (divinylzinc, $sp^2$-hybridized $\mathrm{C}$)
- **III**: $\mathrm{H_3C-CH_2-Zn-CH_2-CH_3}$ (diethylzinc, $sp^3$-hybridized $\mathrm{C}$)

follows the order
questions.explanationEn:
In organozinc compounds, zinc is electropositive ($\chi_{\mathrm{Zn}} \approx 1.65$) relative to carbon, so the bond is polarized as $\mathrm{Zn^{\delta+}-C^{\delta-}}$. The electronegativity of carbon increases with its percentage of $s$-character:
- **I ($sp$, $50\%$ $s$-character):** highest carbon electronegativity ($\chi \approx 3.29$)
- **II ($sp^2$, $33.3\%$ $s$-character):** intermediate carbon electronegativity ($\chi \approx 2.75$)
- **III ($sp^3$, $25\%$ $s$-character):** lowest carbon electronegativity ($\chi \approx 2.48$)

A larger electronegativity difference $\Delta\chi = \chi_{\mathrm{C}} - \chi_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ produces greater $\mathrm{Zn-C}$ bond polarity: $\mathbf{I > II > III}$ — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn: $\mathrm{B_2}$ and $\mathrm{C_2}$, respectively, are
questions.explanationEn:
For second-period homonuclear diatomics up to $\mathrm{N_2}$, $2s\text{--}2p$ mixing places the degenerate $\pi_{2p_x}, \pi_{2p_y}$ MOs below $\sigma_{2p_z}$:
- **$\mathrm{B_2}$ ($10\ e^-$):** $(\sigma_{1s})^2(\sigma^*_{1s})^2(\sigma_{2s})^2(\sigma^*_{2s})^2(\pi_{2p_x})^1(\pi_{2p_y})^1$ $\implies$ **2 unpaired electrons** (by Hund's rule) $\implies$ **paramagnetic**.
- **$\mathrm{C_2}$ ($12\ e^-$):** $(\sigma_{1s})^2(\sigma^*_{1s})^2(\sigma_{2s})^2(\sigma^*_{2s})^2(\pi_{2p_x})^2(\pi_{2p_y})^2$ $\implies$ **0 unpaired electrons** $\implies$ **diamagnetic**.

Hence, $\mathrm{B_2}$ and $\mathrm{C_2}$ are **paramagnetic and diamagnetic**, respectively — Option **(A)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Mobility of ions $\mathrm{Li^+}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$, $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ in water at $298\ \mathrm{K}$ follows the order
questions.explanationEn:
Ionic mobility $u = \frac{\lambda^\circ}{zF}$ in aqueous solution is inversely proportional to the **hydrated ionic radius** (Stokes' law). Smaller bare ions have higher charge density and attract a larger hydration shell, slowing their motion through water.

At $298\ \mathrm{K}$, the limiting molar ionic conductivities $\lambda^\circ$ (in $\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$) are:
- $\mathrm{Li^+}$: $38.7$ (largest hydrated radius $\implies$ lowest mobility)
- $\mathrm{Na^+}$: $50.1$
- $\mathrm{Ag^+}$: $61.9$
- $\mathrm{K^+}$: $73.5$ (smallest hydrated radius $\implies$ highest mobility)

Therefore, the mobility order is $\mathrm{Li^+ < Na^+ < Ag^+ < K^+}$ — Option **(D)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The suitable synthetic route(s) for the following transformation:

cyclopentylmethanol (cyclopentane ring with dashed $\mathrm{H}$ and $-\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C1) $\longrightarrow$ 2-cyclopentylacetic acid (cyclopentane ring with dashed $\mathrm{H}$ and $-\mathrm{CH_2CO_2H}$ at C1)

is/are
optionsEn: (i) *para*-toluenesulfonyl chloride ($\mathrm{TsCl}$), pyridine; (ii) $\mathrm{KCN}$; (iii) conc. aq. $\mathrm{NaOH}$, reflux; (iv) aq. $\mathrm{HCl}$
questions.explanationEn:
Let $\mathrm{R} =$ cyclopentyl. The required transformation is a **one-carbon homologation** of $\mathrm{R-CH_2OH}$ to $\mathrm{R-CH_2CO_2H}$:
- **Option (A) — Grignard carboxylation:** $\mathrm{RCH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{TsCl/py}} \mathrm{RCH_2OTs} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KI}} \mathrm{RCH_2I} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Mg/Et_2O}} \mathrm{RCH_2MgI} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CO_2;\ aq.\ HCl}} \mathrm{RCH_2CO_2H}$. **Correct.**
- **Option (B) — Nitrile homologation:** $\mathrm{RCH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{TsCl/py}} \mathrm{RCH_2OTs} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{RCH_2CN} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH,\ \Delta;\ aq.\ HCl}} \mathrm{RCH_2CO_2H}$. **Correct.**
- **Option (C) — Arndt–Eistert homologation:** $\mathrm{RCH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3/H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{RCO_2H} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{RCOCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_2N_2}} \mathrm{RCOCHN_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Ag_2O,\ H_2O}} \mathrm{RCH_2CO_2H}$ (via Wolff rearrangement of the $\alpha$-diazoketone). **Correct.**
- **Option (D):** Jones oxidation gives $\mathrm{RCO_2H}$, and $\mathrm{CH_2N_2}$ simply methylates it to the methyl ester $\mathrm{RCO_2Me}$ (no carbon-chain homologation). **Incorrect.**

Hence, the correct options are **(A), (B), and (C)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The compound(s) which on reaction with $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ followed by treatment with aqueous $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ would produce 1-methyl-1-phenylethanol as the major product is/are
questions.explanationEn:
The target tertiary alcohol is 1-methyl-1-phenylethanol (2-phenylpropan-2-ol), $\mathrm{Ph-C(CH_3)_2-OH}$:
- **(A) Methyl benzoate ($\mathrm{PhCO_2Me}$):** Reacts with 2 equivalents of $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ (first forming acetophenone, then adding a second methyl group) followed by aq. $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ to give $\mathrm{Ph-C(CH_3)_2-OH}$. **Correct.**
- **(B) Phenyl acetate ($\mathrm{CH_3CO_2Ph}$):** Reacts with 2 equivalents of $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ to give *tert*-butanol ($\mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH}$) and phenol ($\mathrm{PhOH}$). **Incorrect.**
- **(C) Acetaldehyde ($\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$):** Reacts with $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ to give propan-2-ol ($\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHOH}$). **Incorrect.**
- **(D) Acetophenone ($\mathrm{PhCOCH_3}$):** Reacts with 1 equivalent of $\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}$ followed by aq. $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ to give $\mathrm{Ph-C(CH_3)_2-OH}$. **Correct.**

Hence, the correct options are **(A) and (D)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Among the following, the compound(s) which produce the same osazone as that obtained from D-glucose, when reacted with phenylhydrazine, is/are
optionsEn: D-mannose (Fischer projection: $\mathrm{CHO}$ at C1; C2: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C3: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C4: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; C5: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; $\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C6)

D-fructose (Fischer projection: $\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C1; $\mathrm{C=O}$ at C2; C3: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C4: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; C5: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; $\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C6)

D-talose (Fischer projection: $\mathrm{CHO}$ at C1; C2: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C3: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C4: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C5: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; $\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C6)

D-glucitol / D-sorbitol (Fischer projection: $\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C1; C2: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; C3: $\mathrm{HO}$ left, $\mathrm{H}$ right; C4: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; C5: $\mathrm{H}$ left, $\mathrm{OH}$ right; $\mathrm{CH_2OH}$ at C6)
questions.explanationEn:
Osazone formation with excess phenylhydrazine ($\mathrm{PhNHNH_2}$) converts both C1 and C2 into phenylhydrazone groups, destroying the stereocenter at C2. Therefore, any aldohexose or 2-ketohexose that shares the **same stereochemistry at C3, C4, and C5** as D-glucose (C3: $\mathrm{OH}$ left; C4: $\mathrm{OH}$ right; C5: $\mathrm{OH}$ right) yields the **identical glucosazone**:
- **(A) D-Mannose:** C2-epimer of D-glucose; identical at C3, C4, and C5 $\implies$ forms the **same osazone**. **Correct.**
- **(B) D-Fructose:** 2-Ketohexose with identical configurations at C3, C4, and C5 $\implies$ forms the **same osazone**. **Correct.**
- **(C) D-Talose:** Differs at C4 ($\mathrm{OH}$ left) $\implies$ gives a different osazone. **Incorrect.**
- **(D) D-Glucitol (sorbitol):** An alditol lacking any carbonyl group $\implies$ does not react with phenylhydrazine to form an osazone. **Incorrect.**

Hence, the correct options are **(A) and (B)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Among the following, the chiral molecule(s) is/are
optionsEn: spiro[3.3]hepta-1,5-diene (two orthogonal cyclobutene rings sharing a central spiro carbon)
1,3-dichloro-2,4-dimethylcyclobutane with alternating stereochemistry (1-$\mathrm{Cl}$ wedged, 2-$\mathrm{Me}$ dashed, 3-$\mathrm{Cl}$ dashed, 4-$\mathrm{Me}$ wedged)
questions.explanationEn:
A molecule is **chiral** if it lacks all improper axes of rotation $S_n$ (including mirror planes $\sigma = S_1$ and an inversion center $i = S_2$):
- **(A) Spiro[3.3]hepta-1,5-diene:** The two cyclobutene rings lie in mutually perpendicular planes, and each ring is unsymmetrically substituted (one side has a $\mathrm{C=C}$ bond, the other a $\mathrm{CH_2}$). The molecule has $D_2$ symmetry (no $\sigma$, $i$, or $S_n$) $\implies$ **axially chiral**. **Correct.**
- **(B) 1,3-Dichloro-2,4-dimethylcyclobutane (1-wedge $\mathrm{Cl}$, 2-dash $\mathrm{Me}$, 3-dash $\mathrm{Cl}$, 4-wedge $\mathrm{Me}$):** Possesses a center of inversion ($i$) at the center of the cyclobutane ring ($C_i$ symmetry) $\implies$ **achiral**. **Incorrect.**
- **(C) *trans*-4-Methylcyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid:** Possesses a mirror plane ($\sigma$) passing through C1 and C4 ($C_s$ symmetry) $\implies$ **achiral**. **Incorrect.**
- **(D) 2,4-Dichloropenta-2,3-diene:** An evenly substituted allene of the type $ab\mathrm{C=C=C}ab$ ($a = \mathrm{Me} \neq b = \mathrm{Cl}$). Its orthogonal terminal planes eliminate $\sigma$, $i$, and $S_n$ ($C_2$ symmetry) $\implies$ **axially chiral**. **Correct.**

Hence, the correct options are **(A) and (D)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct assumption(s) required to derive Langmuir adsorption isotherm is/are
optionsEn: Adsorption is limited to a monolayer on adsorbing surface.
All binding sites on adsorbing surface are identical.
Adsorption of a molecule on a site enhances binding of other molecules on neighboring sites.
Rate of adsorption and rate of desorption are equal at equilibrium.
questions.explanationEn:
The **Langmuir adsorption isotherm** is derived from the following core assumptions:
1. Adsorption cannot proceed beyond **monolayer** coverage — **(A) is correct**.
2. The adsorbent surface is uniform, meaning **all binding sites are equivalent/identical** with the same enthalpy of adsorption — **(B) is correct**.
3. There are **no lateral interactions** between adsorbed molecules on neighboring sites (occupancy of one site does not affect the binding energy of adjacent sites) — **(C) is incorrect**.
4. A **dynamic equilibrium** is established where the rate of adsorption equals the rate of desorption ($k_a P (1 - \theta) = k_d \theta$) — **(D) is correct**.

Hence, the correct options are **(A), (B), and (D)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
For one mole of an ideal gas, the correct statement(s) is/are

[$U =$ internal energy; $V =$ volume; $T =$ temperature; $P =$ pressure]
questions.explanationEn:
For $1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of an ideal gas ($PV = RT$, and internal energy $U$ depends solely on $T$):
- **(A):** $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P = T\left(\frac{R}{V}\right) - P = 0$. **Correct.**
- **(B):** $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V = C_{V,m} > 0$ (heat capacity at constant volume is always positive). **Correct.**
- **(C):** Since $P = RT/V$, $\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V = \frac{R}{V} > 0$. **Correct.**
- **(D):** Since $V = RT/P$, $\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\frac{RT}{P^2} < 0$ (volume decreases as pressure increases isothermally). **Incorrect.**

Hence, the correct options are **(A), (B), and (C)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the exothermic chemical reaction $\mathrm{O_2}(g) + 2\mathrm{H_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{H_2O}(g)$ at equilibrium in a closed container. The correct statement(s) is/are
optionsEn: At equilibrium, introduction of catalyst increases product formation.
Equilibrium constant decreases with increase in temperature.
The equilibrium constant $K_P$ increases with pressure.
Decrease in volume of reaction vessel increases product formation.
questions.explanationEn:
For the exothermic reaction $\mathrm{O_2}(g) + 2\mathrm{H_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{H_2O}(g)$, we have $\Delta H^\circ < 0$ and $\Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 2) = -1$:
- **(A) Incorrect:** A catalyst lowers the activation energy of forward and reverse reactions equally and does not alter the equilibrium composition.
- **(B) Correct:** By the van 't Hoff equation, $\frac{d\ln K_P}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2} < 0$, so increasing temperature decreases $K_P$.
- **(C) Incorrect:** The equilibrium constant $K_P$ depends solely on temperature, not on total pressure.
- **(D) Correct:** Decreasing the vessel volume increases total pressure; by Le Chatelier's principle, equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas ($\Delta n_g = -1$), increasing $\mathrm{H_2O}(g)$ formation.

Hence, the correct options are **(B) and (D)**.

questions.questionTextEn: Elements and their processes of extraction/purification are given. The correct pair(s) is/are
questions.explanationEn:
Evaluating each element–process pair:
- **(A) $\mathrm{Na}$; Downs process:** Elemental sodium is extracted commercially by the electrolysis of molten $\mathrm{NaCl}$ (mixed with $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ to lower the melting point) in a Downs cell. **Correct.**
- **(B) $\mathrm{Ni}$; Mond process:** Impure nickel is purified via volatile $\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}$ formation at $\sim 50\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ followed by thermal decomposition at $\sim 200\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. **Correct.**
- **(C) $\mathrm{B}$; Frasch process:** The Frasch process extracts elemental **sulfur** ($\mathrm{S}$) from underground deposits, not boron. **Incorrect.**
- **(D) $\mathrm{Al}$; Bayer process:** The Bayer process refines bauxite ore to purified **alumina ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$)**, whereas extraction of elemental **aluminium ($\mathrm{Al}$)** is carried out by the Hall–Héroult electrolytic process (and purification of $\mathrm{Al}$ by Hoope's process). **Incorrect.**

Hence, the correct options are **(A) and (B)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct statement(s) about the ligand substitution/exchange reaction is/are
optionsEn: The rate is faster in the case of $\mathrm{SF_6}$ than in $[\mathrm{AlF_6}]^{3-}$.
The rate is faster in the case of $[\mathrm{Mg(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ than in $[\mathrm{Sr(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$.
The rate of water exchange is faster in the case of $[\mathrm{Ni(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ than in $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5(H_2O)}]^{3+}$.
The rate is faster in case of $[\mathrm{Cr(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ than in $[\mathrm{Cr(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}$.
questions.explanationEn:
Evaluating the kinetic lability of each pair:
- **(A) Incorrect:** $\mathrm{SF_6}$ is famously kinetically inert (small central $\mathrm{S}$ sterically shielded by six $\mathrm{F}$ atoms, high $\mathrm{S-F}$ bond energy), whereas $[\mathrm{AlF_6}]^{3-}$ exchanges fluoride much more readily.
- **(B) Incorrect:** Both $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}$ are $d^0$ alkaline-earth ions, so water-exchange rate depends inversely on charge-to-radius ratio ($z/r$). Because $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ is smaller than $\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}$, it binds $\mathrm{H_2O}$ more tightly, making $[\mathrm{Mg(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ ($k \sim 10^5\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$) *slower* than $[\mathrm{Sr(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ ($k \sim 10^9\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$).
- **(C) Correct:** $[\mathrm{Ni(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ ($d^8$, $k \sim 3 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$) is much more labile than low-spin $d^6$ $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_5(H_2O)}]^{3+}$ (very high LFSE and $+3$ charge, kinetically inert, $k \sim 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$).
- **(D) Correct:** High-spin $d^4$ $[\mathrm{Cr(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ exhibits strong Jahn–Teller elongation of its axial $\mathrm{Cr-O}$ bonds and lower charge ($k \sim 10^9\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$), making it vastly more labile than $d^3$ $[\mathrm{Cr(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}$ (high LFSE, kinetically inert, $k \sim 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$).

Hence, the correct options are **(C) and (D)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The stretching frequency of $\mathrm{CO}$ in $\mathrm{H_3B\cdot CO}$ is
optionsEn: greater than the stretching frequency in free $\mathrm{CO}$.
lesser than the stretching frequency in free $\mathrm{CO}$.
lesser than the stretching frequency of $\mathrm{CO}$ in $\mathrm{Fe(CO)_5}$.
greater than the stretching frequency of $\mathrm{CO}$ in $\mathrm{Fe(CO)_5}$.
questions.explanationEn:
The carbonyl stretching frequency $\nu(\mathrm{CO})$ reflects the strength of the $\mathrm{C\equiv O}$ bond:
1. **In free $\mathrm{CO}$:** $\nu(\mathrm{CO}) = 2143\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The HOMO ($5\sigma$, carbon lone pair) has slight $\mathrm{C-O}$ antibonding character.
2. **In $\mathrm{H_3B\cdot CO}$ (borane carbonyl):** $\mathrm{CO}$ donates electron density from its slightly antibonding $5\sigma$ orbital into the empty $p$-orbital of $\mathrm{BH_3}$, with negligible $\pi$-backbonding from boron. Removing antibonding electron density strengthens the $\mathrm{C-O}$ bond, raising $\nu(\mathrm{CO})$ to **$\sim 2165\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$** (greater than free $\mathrm{CO}$) — **(A) is correct**.
3. **In $\mathrm{Fe(CO)_5}$:** Electron-rich $\mathrm{Fe}(0)$ donates strongly via $d\pi \to \pi^*(\mathrm{CO})$ backbonding, weakening the $\mathrm{C-O}$ bond and lowering $\nu(\mathrm{CO})$ to **$\sim 2000\text{--}2028\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$**. Thus, $\nu(\mathrm{CO})$ in $\mathrm{H_3B\cdot CO}$ is also **greater than** in $\mathrm{Fe(CO)_5}$ — **(D) is correct**.

Hence, the correct options are **(A) and (D)**.

questions.questionTextEn:
For the following compound:

dimethyl terephthalate ($1,4\text{-C}_6\mathrm{H}_4(\mathrm{CO_2CH_3})_2$, a benzene ring substituted at the 1- and 4-positions with $-\mathrm{C(=O)OCH_3}$ ester groups)

the number of signals expected in the $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectrum is _______.
questions.explanationEn:
Dimethyl terephthalate ($1,4\text{-C}_6\mathrm{H}_4(\mathrm{CO_2CH_3})_2$) has high molecular symmetry ($D_{2h}$):
1. All **4 aromatic protons** on the *para*-disubstituted benzene ring are chemically equivalent by symmetry and give **1 singlet** (around $\delta\ 8.1\ \mathrm{ppm}$).
2. All **6 ester methyl protons** (the two $-\mathrm{OCH_3}$ groups) are chemically equivalent and give **1 singlet** (around $\delta\ 3.9\ \mathrm{ppm}$).

Therefore, the total number of $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR signals expected is **$2$**.

questions.questionTextEn:
Exhaustive hydrogenation of the following compound:

$(E)$-6-methyl-4-methylenenon-6-en-2-yne ($\mathrm{CH_3-C\equiv C-C(=CH_2)-CH_2-C(CH_3)=CH-CH_2CH_3}$)

under $\mathrm{Pd/C}$ generates a saturated hydrocarbon as the product. The number of stereoisomers possible for this product is _______.
questions.explanationEn:
Exhaustive catalytic hydrogenation ($\mathrm{H_2, Pd/C}$) saturates the C2$\equiv$C3 alkyne, the exocyclic C4$=\mathrm{CH_2}$ alkene, and the C6$=$C7 alkene, converting the substrate into the saturated alkane:
$$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2-\overset{*}{C}H(CH_3)-CH_2-\overset{*}{C}H(CH_3)-CH_2CH_2CH_3} \quad (\text{4,6-dimethylnonane})$$
4,6-Dimethylnonane contains **2 identically substituted stereocenters** (C4 and C6, each bonded to $-\mathrm{H}$, $-\mathrm{CH_3}$, $-\mathrm{CH_2CH_2CH_3}$, and the rest of the chain). Its possible stereoisomers are:
1. $(4R, 6R)$ and $(4S, 6S)$ — an enantiomeric pair (2 optically active stereoisomers).
2. $(4R, 6S) \equiv (4S, 6R)$ — a single achiral **meso** compound (internal plane of symmetry passing through C5).

Thus, the total number of possible stereoisomers is **$3$**.

questions.questionTextEn:
For a zero-order reaction $\mathrm{P \to Q}$, the concentration of $\mathrm{P}$ becomes half of its initial concentration in $30\ \mathrm{minutes}$ after starting the reaction.

The concentration of $\mathrm{P}$ becomes zero at _______ minutes. *(rounded off to the nearest integer)*
questions.explanationEn:
For a **zero-order reaction** $\mathrm{P \to Q}$, the integrated rate law is $[\mathrm{P}]_t = [\mathrm{P}]_0 - kt$.
- Half-life: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{P}]_0}{2k} = 30\ \mathrm{min}$.
- Completion time ($[\mathrm{P}]_t = 0$): $t_{\text{completion}} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{P}]_0}{k} = 2\,t_{1/2} = 2 \times 30 = 60\ \mathrm{min}$.

Hence, the concentration of $\mathrm{P}$ becomes zero at **$60$** minutes.

questions.questionTextEn:
The magnitude of energy difference between the energy levels $n = 3$ and $n = 2$ of a quantum particle of mass $m$ in a box of length $L$ is $\dfrac{Xh^2}{8mL^2}$. Then $X =$ _______.

*(rounded off to the nearest integer)*

[Given: $h$ is Planck's constant and $n$ denotes the quantum number]
questions.explanationEn:
The energy of a particle of mass $m$ in a 1D box of length $L$ in level $n$ is:
$$E_n = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8mL^2}$$
The energy difference between $n = 3$ and $n = 2$ is:
$$\Delta E = E_3 - E_2 = (3^2 - 2^2)\frac{h^2}{8mL^2} = (9 - 4)\frac{h^2}{8mL^2} = \frac{5h^2}{8mL^2}$$
Comparing with $\dfrac{Xh^2}{8mL^2}$, we obtain $X =$ **$5$**.

questions.questionTextEn: The function $\exp(-2(x - 1)^2)$ attains a maximum at $x =$ _______. *(rounded off to the nearest integer)*
questions.explanationEn:
Let $f(x) = \exp(-2(x - 1)^2)$. Since the exponential function $\exp(u)$ is strictly increasing with $u$, $f(x)$ attains its maximum where the exponent $u(x) = -2(x - 1)^2$ is maximized.
Because $(x - 1)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, $-2(x - 1)^2 \le 0$, with the maximum value $0$ occurring uniquely at $x - 1 = 0 \implies x = 1$.

Equivalently, setting the first derivative to zero:
$$f'(x) = -4(x - 1)\exp(-2(x - 1)^2) = 0 \implies x = 1$$
and $f''(1) = -4 < 0$ confirms a maximum at $x =$ **$1$**.

questions.questionTextEn: $0.1\ \mathrm{M}$ aqueous solution of a weak monobasic acid has $\mathrm{pH}\ 2.0$. The $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of the monobasic acid is _______. *(rounded off to one decimal place)*
questions.explanationEn:
For a weak monobasic acid $\mathrm{HA} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{A^-}$ with initial concentration $C = 0.1\ \mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{pH} = 2.0$:
$$[\mathrm{H^+}] = [\mathrm{A^-}] = 10^{-2.0} = 0.01\ \mathrm{M}$$
Using the exact equilibrium expression:
$$K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{C - [\mathrm{H^+}]} = \frac{(0.01)^2}{0.1 - 0.01} = \frac{10^{-4}}{0.09} = 1.111 \times 10^{-3}$$
$$\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log_{10}(1.111 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.954 \approx 3.0$$
(Note: Using the dilute-acid approximation $K_a \approx [\mathrm{H^+}]^2/C = 10^{-3}$ also gives $\mathrm{p}K_a = 3.0$; the official answer key accepts **$2.9$ to $3.0$**.)

questions.questionTextEn:
The enthalpy change for the reaction

$\mathrm{C}(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) \to \mathrm{CO}(g)$ is _______ $\mathrm{kJ}$ per mole of $\mathrm{CO}(g)$ produced.

*(rounded off to one decimal place)*

[Given:
$\mathrm{C}(g) + \mathrm{O_2}(g) \to \mathrm{CO_2}(g),\ \Delta H_{\text{rxn}} = -393.5\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per mole of $\mathrm{CO_2}(g)$ produced
$\mathrm{CO_2}(g) \to \mathrm{CO}(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g),\ \Delta H_{\text{rxn}} = 283.0\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per mole of $\mathrm{CO}(g)$ produced]
questions.explanationEn:
Applying **Hess's law** of constant heat summation, add the two given thermochemical equations directly:
1. $\mathrm{C}(g) + \mathrm{O_2}(g) \to \mathrm{CO_2}(g), \quad \Delta H_1 = -393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$
2. $\mathrm{CO_2}(g) \to \mathrm{CO}(g) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g), \quad \Delta H_2 = +283.0\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$

Summing (1) and (2) cancels $\mathrm{CO_2}(g)$ and $\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g)$:
$$\mathrm{C}(g) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) \to \mathrm{CO}(g)$$
$$\Delta H_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 = -393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$$
Hence, the enthalpy change is **$-110.5$** $\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$ (official key range: $-111.0$ to $-110.0$).

questions.questionTextEn: The $\mathrm{N-O}$ bond order in $[\mathrm{NO}]^-$ is _______.
questions.explanationEn:
The nitroxyl anion $[\mathrm{NO}]^-$ has $7 + 8 + 1 = 16$ total electrons (12 valence electrons), making it isoelectronic with $\mathrm{O_2}$. Its valence molecular orbital configuration is:
$$(\sigma_{2s})^2(\sigma^*_{2s})^2(\sigma_{2p_z})^2(\pi_{2p_x})^2(\pi_{2p_y})^2(\pi^*_{2p_x})^1(\pi^*_{2p_y})^1$$
Here, the number of bonding electrons is $N_b = 8$ and antibonding electrons is $N_a = 4$ (valence count; or $10$ and $6$ including $1s$):
$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2} = \frac{8 - 4}{2} = 2$$
Hence, the $\mathrm{N-O}$ bond order in $[\mathrm{NO}]^-$ is **$2$**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The bond length of $\mathrm{CO}$ is $113\ \mathrm{pm}$ and its dipole moment ($\vec{\mu}$) is $0.1\ \mathrm{D}$. The charge (in units of electronic charge) on carbon in the $\mathrm{CO}$ molecule *including its sign* is _______. *(rounded off to three decimal places)*

[Given: charge of electron $= 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; $1\ \mathrm{D} = 3.336 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}$]
questions.explanationEn:
The magnitude of the partial charge $q$ (in coulombs) is calculated from $\mu = q\,d$:
- $\mu = 0.1\ \mathrm{D} = 0.1 \times 3.336 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m} = 3.336 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{C\ m}$
- $d = 113\ \mathrm{pm} = 113 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
$$|q| = \frac{\mu}{d} = \frac{3.336 \times 10^{-31}}{113 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.9522 \times 10^{-21}\ \mathrm{C}$$
In units of elementary electronic charge $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$:
$$\frac{|q|}{e} = \frac{2.9522 \times 10^{-21}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.01843 \approx 0.018$$
**Sign of charge on carbon:** In $\mathrm{CO}$, the triple-bonded resonance structure $^-\mathrm{C\equiv O}^+$ dominates (due to the dative $\pi$-bond from oxygen to carbon), so the net dipole moment points from $\mathrm{O}$ toward $\mathrm{C}$, giving **carbon a small negative partial charge**.

Therefore, the charge on carbon is **$-0.018$** (official key range: $-0.019$ to $-0.017$).

questions.questionTextEn: The magnetic moment of $\mathrm{O_3}$ molecule is _______ Bohr magneton (B.M.). *(rounded off to the nearest integer)*
questions.explanationEn:
Ozone ($\mathrm{O_3}$) has $3 \times 6 = 18$ valence electrons (an even number), all of which are **paired** in its bent ($C_{2v}$) singlet ground state (resonance hybrid of $\mathrm{O=O^+-O^-} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{^-O-O^+=O}$). With $n = 0$ unpaired electrons, $\mathrm{O_3}$ is **diamagnetic**, so its spin-only magnetic moment is:
$$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \mathrm{B.M.} = 0\ \mathrm{B.M.}$$
Hence, the magnetic moment is **$0$** B.M.

questions.questionTextEn:
A reaction of $10.50\ \mathrm{g}$ of 1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-dione with conc. $\mathrm{NaOH}$ followed by aqueous acidic work-up furnished $8.55\ \mathrm{g}$ of a carboxylic acid. The yield of the carboxylic acid in this reaction is _______ $\%$.

*(rounded off to the nearest integer)*
questions.explanationEn:
Treatment of 1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-dione (**benzil**, $\mathrm{Ph-CO-CO-Ph}$, formula $\mathrm{C_{14}H_{10}O_2}$) with conc. $\mathrm{NaOH}$ followed by acidic work-up is the **benzilic acid rearrangement**, producing **benzilic acid** (2-hydroxy-2,2-diphenylacetic acid, $\mathrm{Ph_2C(OH)CO_2H}$, formula $\mathrm{C_{14}H_{12}O_3}$) in a $1:1$ molar ratio:
- Molar mass of benzil ($\mathrm{C_{14}H_{10}O_2}$) $= 14(12) + 10(1) + 2(16) = 210\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$
- Molar mass of benzilic acid ($\mathrm{C_{14}H_{12}O_3}$) $= 14(12) + 12(1) + 3(16) = 228\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$
- Moles of benzil $= \dfrac{10.50\ \mathrm{g}}{210\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$
- Theoretical mass of benzilic acid $= 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol} \times 228\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} = 11.40\ \mathrm{g}$
$$\text{Percentage yield} = \frac{8.55\ \mathrm{g}}{11.40\ \mathrm{g}} \times 100\% = 75.0\%$$
Hence, the yield is **$75$** $\%$ (official key range: $74$ to $76$).

questions.questionTextEn: The specific rotation of an optically pure compound is $+75.3$ ($c\ 1.0$ in $\mathrm{CHCl_3}$) at $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A synthetic sample of the same compound showed a specific rotation of $+66.3$ ($c\ 1.0$ in $\mathrm{CHCl_3}$) at $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The enantiomeric excess ($ee$) of the synthetic sample is _______ $\%$. *(rounded off to the nearest integer)*
questions.explanationEn:
Under identical solvent, concentration, and temperature conditions, the enantiomeric excess ($ee$) equals the optical purity:
$$ee = \frac{[\alpha]_{\text{observed}}}{[\alpha]_{\text{pure}}} \times 100\% = \frac{+66.3}{+75.3} \times 100\% = 88.05\% \approx 88\%$$
Hence, the enantiomeric excess is **$88$** $\%$.

questions.questionTextEn:
A salt $\mathrm{QCl}$ of a certain metal $\mathrm{Q}$ is electrolyzed to its elements. $40\ \mathrm{g}$ of metal $\mathrm{Q}$ is formed at an electrode. The volume of $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ formed at the other electrode at $1\ \mathrm{atm}$ pressure and $298\ \mathrm{K}$ is _______ litres. *(rounded off to one decimal place)*

[Given: The gas constant $R = 0.082\ \mathrm{L\ atm\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}}$, the molar mass of $\mathrm{Q}$ is $40\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ is assumed to be an ideal gas]
questions.explanationEn:
Electrolysis of $\mathrm{QCl}$ follows the stoichiometry:
$$\mathrm{QCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Q} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2}(g)$$
- Moles of $\mathrm{Q}$ deposited $= \dfrac{40\ \mathrm{g}}{40\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ (requiring $1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of electrons).
- Moles of $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ evolved at the anode $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.0 = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol}$.
Using the ideal gas law $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$ at $P = 1\ \mathrm{atm}$ and $T = 298\ \mathrm{K}$:
$$V = \frac{0.5 \times 0.082 \times 298}{1} = 12.218\ \mathrm{L} \approx 12.2\ \mathrm{L}$$
Hence, the volume of $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ formed is **$12.2$** litres (official key range: $12.1$ to $12.3$).

questions.questionTextEn:
If $1\ \mathrm{M}$ of a dye in water transmits $50\%$ of incident light at $400\ \mathrm{nm}$, then $2\ \mathrm{M}$ of the dye in water transmits _______ $\%$ of the incident light at $400\ \mathrm{nm}$. *(rounded off to the nearest integer)*

[Given: Both experiments are performed in the same spectrophotometric cell.]
questions.explanationEn:
By the **Beer–Lambert law**, absorbance $A = -\log_{10} T = \varepsilon c l$, where $T$ is transmittance ($0 \le T \le 1$). In the same cell ($l$ constant) at the same wavelength ($\varepsilon$ constant), doubling the concentration from $c_1 = 1\ \mathrm{M}$ to $c_2 = 2\ \mathrm{M}$ doubles the absorbance:
$$A_2 = 2A_1 \implies -\log_{10} T_2 = 2(-\log_{10} T_1) = -\log_{10}(T_1^2)$$
$$T_2 = T_1^2 = (0.50)^2 = 0.25 \equiv 25\%$$
Hence, the $2\ \mathrm{M}$ solution transmits **$25$** $\%$ of the incident light.

questions.questionTextEn:
A $1.0\ \mathrm{L}$ solution is prepared by dissolving $2.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of benzoic acid and $4.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of sodium benzoate in water. The $\mathrm{pH}$ of the resulting solution is _______. *(rounded off to one decimal place)*

Given:
Molar mass of benzoic acid is $122\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$
Molar mass of sodium benzoate is $144\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$
$\mathrm{p}K_a$ of benzoic acid is $4.2$
questions.explanationEn:
This solution is an acidic buffer of benzoic acid ($\mathrm{HA}$) and sodium benzoate ($\mathrm{A^-}$) in $1.0\ \mathrm{L}$:
- $n_{\text{acid}} = \dfrac{2.0\ \mathrm{g}}{122\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.01639\ \mathrm{mol}$
- $n_{\text{salt}} = \dfrac{4.0\ \mathrm{g}}{144\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.02778\ \mathrm{mol}$

Applying the **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation**:
$$\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log_{10}\left(\frac{n_{\text{salt}}}{n_{\text{acid}}}\right) = 4.2 + \log_{10}\left(\frac{0.02778}{0.01639}\right) = 4.2 + \log_{10}(1.6944)$$
$$\mathrm{pH} = 4.2 + 0.2290 = 4.429 \approx 4.4$$
Hence, the $\mathrm{pH}$ of the resulting solution is **$4.4$** (official key range: $4.4$ to $4.5$).

questions.questionTextEn: The total vapour pressure of an ideal binary liquid mixture of benzene and toluene is $0.3\ \mathrm{bar}$. The vapour pressure of pure benzene is $0.5\ \mathrm{bar}$ and that of toluene is $0.2\ \mathrm{bar}$. The mole fraction of benzene in this mixture is _______. *(rounded off to two decimal places)*
questions.explanationEn:
For an ideal binary liquid mixture obeying **Raoult's law**:
$$P_{\text{total}} = x_B P_B^\circ + (1 - x_B) P_T^\circ$$
Substituting $P_{\text{total}} = 0.3\ \mathrm{bar}$, $P_B^\circ = 0.5\ \mathrm{bar}$, and $P_T^\circ = 0.2\ \mathrm{bar}$:
$$0.3 = 0.5\,x_B + 0.2(1 - x_B) = 0.2 + 0.3\,x_B$$
$$x_B = \frac{0.3 - 0.2}{0.3} = \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.33$$
Hence, the mole fraction of benzene is **$0.33$** (official key range: $0.32$ to $0.34$).

questions.questionTextEn:
The unit cell of a two-dimensional square lattice with lattice parameter $a$ is formed by connecting the centers of four mutually touching grey circles of radius $r$ (so that adjacent circles touch along each edge of the dashed square of side $a = 2r$, with one quarter-circle inside each of the four corners of the unit cell).

The percentage ($\%$) area occupied by the grey circles (of radius $r$) inside the unit cell is _______. *(rounded off to the nearest integer)*
questions.explanationEn:
In a 2D primitive square lattice of touching circles of radius $r$:
- Lattice parameter (side of the square unit cell): $a = 2r$, so $\text{Area}_{\text{cell}} = a^2 = 4r^2$.
- Number of circles inside the unit cell: $4 \text{ corners} \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ full circle, so $\text{Area}_{\text{circles}} = \pi r^2$.
$$\text{Packing percentage} = \frac{\pi r^2}{4r^2} \times 100\% = \frac{\pi}{4} \times 100\% = 78.54\% \approx 79\%$$
Hence, the percentage area occupied is **$79$** $\%$ (official key range: $77$ to $79$).

questions.questionTextEn:
In the oxidation of phosphorus with oxygen, $0.2\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{P_4}$ produces _______ $\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$.

*(rounded off to one decimal place)*

[Given: Atomic weight of $\mathrm{P} = 31$; Atomic weight of $\mathrm{O} = 16$]
questions.explanationEn:
The balanced oxidation reaction is:
$$\mathrm{P_4} + 5\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$$
- From the $1:1$ stoichiometry, $0.2\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{P_4}$ produces $0.2\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$.
- Molar mass of $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}} = 4(31) + 10(16) = 124 + 160 = 284\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$.
- Mass of $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}} = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol} \times 284\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} = 56.8\ \mathrm{g}$.

Hence, **$56.8$** $\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$ is produced (official key range: $56.7$ to $56.9$).

questions.questionTextEn:
An element $\mathrm{E}$ has three isotopes:

$^{28}_{14}\mathrm{E}$ (abundance $92.21\%$, atomic mass: $27.977\ \mathrm{a.m.u.}$),
$^{29}_{14}\mathrm{E}$ (abundance $4.70\%$, atomic mass: $28.976\ \mathrm{a.m.u.}$), and
$^{30}_{14}\mathrm{E}$ (abundance $3.09\%$, atomic mass: $29.974\ \mathrm{a.m.u.}$).

The atomic mass of $\mathrm{E}$ is _______ $\mathrm{a.m.u.}$ *(rounded off to three decimal places)*
questions.explanationEn:
The weighted average atomic mass of element $\mathrm{E}$ (silicon) is:
$$M_{\mathrm{E}} = \sum_i f_i m_i = (0.9221 \times 27.977) + (0.0470 \times 28.976) + (0.0309 \times 29.974)$$
$$M_{\mathrm{E}} = 25.79759 + 1.36187 + 0.92620 = 28.08566\ \mathrm{a.m.u.} \approx 28.086\ \mathrm{a.m.u.}$$
Hence, the atomic mass of $\mathrm{E}$ is **$28.086$** $\mathrm{a.m.u.}$ (official key range: $28.082$ to $28.089$).

questions.questionTextEn:
The wavelength of the $\gamma$-ray emitted in

$^{137m}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} \rightsquigarrow {}^{137}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + \gamma\text{-ray}\ (0.66\ \mathrm{MeV})$

is _______ $\text{\AA}$. *(rounded off to three decimal places)*

[Given: $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\ s}$; $c = 2.998 \times 10^8\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$; $1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$]
questions.explanationEn:
Convert the $\gamma$-ray photon energy to joules:
$$E = 0.66\ \mathrm{MeV} \times 1.602 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J\ MeV^{-1}} = 1.05732 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$$
Using $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, the wavelength is:
$$\lambda = \frac{hc}{E} = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 2.998 \times 10^8}{1.05732 \times 10^{-13}} = 1.8788 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$$
Since $1\ \text{\AA} = 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$:
$$\lambda = 1.8788 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{\AA} = 0.01879\ \text{\AA} \approx 0.019\ \text{\AA}$$
Hence, the wavelength of the emitted $\gamma$-ray is **$0.019$** $\text{\AA}$ (official key range: $0.017$ to $0.021$).
